evidence.finding: Billing queue skill mappings were updated at 09:15, exactly when the incident began.
At 09:15, Billing staffed agents fell from 12 to 9 while General Service increased from 19 to 22; those levels persisted through 11:45.
Billing service level fell from 90.5% at 09:00 to 14.8% at 09:15 and remained frequently far below target, while General Service stayed approximately 94.4%-97.1% after the change.
Billing offered 29 calls but answered only 15 at 09:15, and offered 31 but answered 18 at 09:30; Billing ASA rose to 131.2 and 117.2 seconds respectively.
Overall service level dropped from 93.0% at 09:00 to 67.1% at 09:15 and 59.1% at 09:30, with repeated below-target intervals afterward.
Scheduled and logged-in staffing remained constant at 49 throughout the window, with 44-46 productive agents and no training assignments.

Actual demand exceeded forecast at incident onset—87 versus 79 calls at 09:15 and 96 versus 79 at 09:30—amplifying the routing-created Billing constraint but not explaining the persistent queue divergence.
Aggregate AHT and transfer rates did not show a sustained increase coincident with the incident; AHT was generally at or below forecast and transfer rates remained near 6%.

primary_root_cause_detail: The 09:15 Billing skill-mapping change redistributed three staffed agents from Billing to General Service, reducing Billing staffing from 12 to 9 while General Service rose from 19 to 22. Billing then experienced severe, sustained queue-local degradation despite stable total headcount, indicating that the routing configuration created a localized capacity imbalance rather than an enterprise-wide staffing shortage.
recommended_actions: Rollback or correct the 09:15 Billing skill-mapping change and validate all affected agent-skill assignments.
Restore sufficient Billing coverage, including the three agents shifted to General Service, and monitor Billing backlog, ASA, and service level during recovery.
Add pre-deployment validation for queue staffing distribution and skill eligibility, with alerts for abrupt queue-level staffing changes.
Require post-change monitoring and automatic rollback criteria when a routing update causes material queue-level service divergence.
Review forecast-overage contingency rules so temporary cross-skilled capacity can be directed to Billing during moderate demand increases.

rejected_hypotheses.reason: Volume was moderately above forecast at onset, but later varied above and below forecast. It does not explain the exact-timestamp staffing redistribution or why Billing deteriorated while General Service remained strong.
Total scheduled and logged-in headcount remained fixed at 49 and productive staffing stayed within 44-46 agents; the shortage was localized to Billing through redistribution.
Aggregate AHT did not rise materially and was often below forecast; Billing AHT also did not remain elevated enough to explain the sustained service failure.
Adherence remained in its existing 89.8%-93.9% range and did not decline at incident onset.
Agents in training were zero throughout the evaluation window.
No platform event was supplied, and the sharply queue-specific impact aligned with a documented routing configuration change.
Forecast variance contributed at onset but was not sustained and cannot account for the simultaneous transfer of staffing capacity away from Billing.
The reported aggregate service-level values reconcile to the supplied formula, and offered-call counts reconcile with answered plus abandoned calls.
Queue imbalance is an immediate mechanism, but the deeper evidenced cause is the Billing routing configuration change that created the imbalance.

stakeholder_summary: CC-005 was caused by the 09:15 Billing routing change, which shifted three staffed agents from Billing to General Service and created a localized Billing capacity imbalance. Moderate above-forecast demand amplified the initial impact, but stable total staffing, normal AHT, and strong General Service performance rule out an enterprise-wide staffing, handle-time, or platform problem.
